etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English tiren, tirien, teorien, from Old English tȳrian, tēorian (“to fail, cease, become weary, be tired, exhausted; tire, weary, exhaust”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Proto-West Germanic *teuʀōn (“to cease”), which is possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dews- (“to fail, be behind, lag”). Compare Ancient Greek δεύομαι (deúomai, “to lack”), Sanskrit दोष (dóṣa, “crime, fault, vice, deficiency”).

quote.citation: 2012 September 7, Phil McNulty, “Moldova 0-5 England”, in BBC Sport‎[1]:
quote.text: As Moldova understandably tired after a night of ball chasing, Everton left-back Baines scored his first international goal as his deflected free-kick totally wrong-footed Namasco.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Believed from Middle English tire (“equipment”) aphetic form of attire; see details at tyre. See also German zieren (“to decorate”).

definitions.definition: (American spelling, Canadian spelling) alternative spelling of tyre: The rubber covering on a wheel.
(American spelling) alternative spelling of tyre: The metal rim of a wheel, especially that of a railroad locomotive.
A child's apron covering the upper part of the body, and tied with tape or cord; a pinafore. Also tier.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English tire, from Old French tirer (“to draw or pull”), akin to English tear (“to rend”).

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To seize, pull, and tear prey, as a hawk does.

quote.citation: 1593, [William Shakespeare], Venus and Adonis, London:  […]  Richard Field, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Even as an empty eagle, sharp by fast, / Tires with her beak on feathers, flesh, and bone.

quote.text: I grieve myself / To think, when thou shalt be disedged by her / That now thou tirest on, how thy memory / Will then be pang'd by me.

quote.citation: 1612–1613, Nathan Field, John Fletcher, Philip Massinger, “The Honest Mans Fortune”, in Comedies and Tragedies […], London:  […]  Humphrey Robinson, […], and for Humphrey Moseley […], published 1647, →OCLC, Act II, scene v:

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To seize, rend, or tear something as prey; to be fixed upon, or engaged with, anything.
